title: Ansel and the Harvest
premise: Orsen Amberdale, a pest controller who prides himself on never believing in anything he can't trap or poison, is called to Amberdale House — a farmhouse that shares his surname and shouldn't exist on any map. Inside, every mirror lags one second behind reality, and the lag is growing. The house's last resident, Ansel, was swallowed by something with human fingerprints that survives by learning people's names and singing their lives back to them; the only escape is the song's final verse, which must be learned without ever singing along. Orsen discovers the entity has been wearing his family's faces for generations, and that his own survival demands betraying the one person inside who still remembers being human. In the end, Orsen sings the verse alone, trading his reflection for Ansel's freedom — and walks out of the house as a man no mirror will ever acknowledge again.
about_author: Lior Okonkwo is the pen name of a former rural building inspector who spent a decade documenting houses no county would claim. They write horror about paperwork, inheritance, and the terrible arithmetic of staying alive.

chapters.title: The Call Sheet
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. A pest-control dispatcher sends Orsen to a job with no address, only coordinates and a note: 'something with fingerprints.' He mocks it aloud to his partner, establishing his creed of disbelief. Emotional beat: cocky routine before the fall.

chapters.title: A House With His Name
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. The farmhouse bears an amberdale family crest identical to his grandmother's locket. The door opens before he knocks. Beat: unease dressed as coincidence.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Ceiling
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Dust shows handprints pressed into every surface — from the inside of walls. No droppings, no nests, no animal sign. Beat: professional confidence beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Client Who Isn't There
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. A woman's voice gives him instructions through a wall grate but never appears. She calls him by his childhood nickname. Beat: the first violation of his skepticism.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. He catches his reflection moving after him — a full second behind, then catching up. He blames fatigue. Beat: denial hardening into obsession.

chapters.title: The Song Under the Floor
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Something below the floorboards hums a lullaby his mother sang, note-perfect, including the parts she got wrong. Beat: grief weaponized.

chapters.title: Ansel's Room
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. He finds a boy's bedroom preserved mid-life: homework half-done, shoes pointing toward the window. A name carved in the sill — ANSEL AMBERDALE. Beat: dread acquiring a face.

chapters.title: The Verse That Stops
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. The humming always halts at the same line, leaving a silence shaped like a question. Orsen realizes the song is incomplete — and wants completing. Beat: curiosity as bait.

chapters.title: Locked In
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Every exit is gone when he turns around; windows show daylight from the wrong season. His phone reflects a call already ended. Beat: panic contained by stubbornness.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Scratched into a pantry door: three rules — don't sing along, don't answer to your name, don't look for the singer. Beat: the horror becomes a game with stakes.

chapters.title: The Second Reflection
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Mirrors now lag two seconds, and one shows a room he isn't standing in. Beat: the house is editing reality ahead of him.

chapters.title: What the Grate Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. The voice behind the grate admits she was hired to exterminate something once, decades ago. She never left. Beat: foreshadowing his own fate.

chapters.title: Names Have Weight
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. The house whispers 'Orsen' in his mother's voice; answering feels like stepping off a ledge. He bites his tongue silent. Beat: loyalty to self vs. longing to respond.

chapters.title: Ansel, Found
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Behind a mirror, he finds a living boy — thin, gray-eyed, humming. Ansel has been here since 1961, kept because he never finished learning the song. Beat: hope, immediately suspect.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Won't Say His Own Name
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. First chapter from inside. Ansel explains: the entity learns you through your name and your song; he gave both away to survive, and lost himself. Beat: the price of survival made flesh.

chapters.title: Fingerprinted Souls
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. The thing doesn't eat bodies; it presses its prints into identities until they fit its hands. Ansel shows Orsen the wall where previous victims' names are worn smooth. Beat: scale of the horror revealed.

chapters.title: The Last Verse Exists
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. The song has a final verse that ends it — but whoever sings it becomes the house's new keeper unless they've learned it without singing along even once. Beat: rules tighten around the solution.

chapters.title: Practice in Silence
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Ansel teaches him the verse mouthed, soundless, over days that don't pass. Orsen's reflection stops appearing at all. Beat: discipline versus terror.

chapters.title: The House Learns Back
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. The entity begins singing ORSEN's life back at him — his father's funeral, his failures — trying to make him harmonize involuntarily. Beat: identity under siege.

chapters.title: Betrayal Drafted
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. The entity offers Ansel his name back if he delivers Orsen's. Ansel, starving for himself, doesn't say no. Beat: loyalty cracking under want.

chapters.title: The Wrong Lullaby
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. He wakes mouthing the verse aloud — someone sang it to him in his sleep. One slip may have cost everything. Beat: despair and self-doubt.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Mirror
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Trapped facing a mirror, he watches a version of himself answer to his name, smile, and walk deeper into the house. Beat: confronting what surrender looks like.

chapters.title: Ansel's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. Ansel admits he led others here before, hoping each would finish the song and free him. Orsen is just the newest key. Beat: betrayal confessed, trust shattered.

chapters.title: The Woman Behind the Grate
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. He finally opens the grate: the client is a hollowed shape still wearing her work uniform, mouthing instructions she was given in 1974. Beat: pity curdling into resolve.

chapters.title: Two Seconds, Then None
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. The mirrors stop lagging entirely — they now show events before they happen. Orsen sees himself singing. Beat: fatalism closing in.

chapters.title: The Choice Offered
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. The entity speaks plainly through his father's voice: sing the verse with Ansel together, share the keeping, survive. Beat: temptation with a rational face.

chapters.title: Why Orsen Never Believed
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Flashback: believing killed his mother — she followed a song into a well. Disbelief was armor. Now armor must come off. Beat: theme crystallized.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. Ansel weighs delivering Orsen against a century of erasure, and finds he cannot remember why he wanted his name back more than company. Beat: loyalty rekindled at the brink.

chapters.title: The Hunt Through Amberdale House
chapters.summary: POV alternating. The entity hunts them room to room, singing in both their mothers' voices. They run hand in hand like children. Beat: pure kinetic fear.

chapters.title: The Room of Finished Songs
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. They find where completed verses go: rows of open mouths in the wallpaper, all still humming. Beat: the cost of failure made visible.

chapters.title: One Mouth Stopped
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. Ansel silences one mouth — the 1974 exterminator — by speaking her forgotten name back to her. She crumbles, grateful. Beat: names as mercy, not just danger.

chapters.title: The Verse Completed
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Orsen realizes he knows the ending not from teaching but from memory: his mother's song was this song. He was born into the debt. Beat: revelation recontextualizing everything.

chapters.title: Singing Alone
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. At the hearth, Orsen sings the final verse solo while the entity wears every face he loves, begging in chorus. He does not harmonize. Beat: climax — will against hunger.

chapters.title: What the Prints Let Go
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. The fingerprints lift off the world like wet paint peeling. The house exhales. Ansel feels his own name return like heat. Beat: release after pressure.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Vacancy
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. The house needs a keeper or it dies screaming. Ansel chooses to stay — freely, named, whole — so Orsen can leave. Beat: sacrifice inverted from earlier betrayal.

chapters.title: Exit Without a Reflection
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Orsen walks out at dawn. Shop windows, car mirrors, still water: none of them hold him anymore. Beat: bittersweet victory, the price tallied.

chapters.title: The Report He Can't File
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Back at the office, no record of the job exists. His dispatcher has never heard of Amberdale. Only the invoice remains, paid in old currency. Beat: gaslight epilogue.

chapters.title: Humming at the Window
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Months later, Orsen hears humming outside his flat — the song, complete now, sung gently. He doesn't open the curtain. He taps the rhythm back twice: thank you. Beat: grief turned to communion.

chapters.title: The New Exterminator
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. In the house, Ansel trains a frightened newcomer in the rules, kind where the entity was cruel. The house is changing hands into something gentler. Beat: cycle bent, not broken.

chapters.title: Amberdale, Unmirrored
chapters.summary: POV Orsen, final. Orsen visits his mother's grave and finally says his own name aloud, unafraid. Somewhere far off, a song finishes without him. Beat: resolution — identity reclaimed at the cost of reflection, truth chosen over survival's easy lie.
